slides.title: What is 'Closing the Gap'?
slides.hint: Hover a highlighted key term for its definition. Tap 'Reveal notes' for the lines to record.
body: We acknowledge the Traditional Custodians of the land on which we learn, and pay our respects to Elders past and present. This lesson discusses the health and wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and we approach it with respect.

[[Closing the Gap is a national plan to reach equality in health and wellbeing between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and other Australians.]] It began as a government commitment in 2008.

In 2020, governments signed a new National Agreement on Closing the Gap, this time in partnership with the ==Coalition of Peaks==. [[The 2020 Agreement expanded the original seven targets to around nineteen, covering health, education, jobs, housing, justice, land and culture.]]
The Agreement is built on four ==Priority Reforms==. [[Solutions work best when they are community-led, through shared decision-making and stronger Aboriginal Community-Controlled organisations.]]

keyTerms.definition: A group of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community-controlled organisations that negotiates with governments on equal footing.
The four changes to the way governments work — shared decision-making, building community-controlled organisations, transforming government, and shared data — that underpin the 2020 Agreement.

slides.title: Is the Gap Closing? (BTN)

summary.title: Before you watch
summary.body: ⚠ Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander viewers are advised this story contains images of people who have died. This clip is from 2016 — as you watch, think about whether things have improved since then. We will check it against today's data in the next sections.

slides.urlMeta: Behind the News, ABC · opens in a new tab

slides.title: Watch & respond: Is the Gap Closing?

source.label: Source — 'Is the Gap Closing?', Behind the News (ABC, 2016)
source.transcript: A short news explainer on the Closing the Gap targets and whether Australia was on track to meet them in 2016.

provenance.label: Purpose
provenance.value: To explain Closing the Gap to students

slides.intro: Answer each task in your own words, then reveal the model response.

tasks.question: According to the clip, what does 'Closing the Gap' aim to achieve?
tasks.model: It aims to reach equality in health and life outcomes between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and other Australians.

tasks.question: Name two areas of life where the gap is measured.
tasks.model: Any two of: life expectancy, child mortality, education, employment, reading and numeracy.

tasks.question: The clip is from 2016. Based on it, was Australia on track to close the gap? Give one example.
tasks.model: Mostly no — in 2016 most targets were not on track. For example, the life-expectancy target was not being met. (We will test whether this has improved using current data next.)

slides.title: The life expectancy gap

source.label: Source A — Life expectancy at birth, 2020–2022 (animated chart embeds here)
source.transcript: Babies born 2020–2022, average life expectancy: First Nations males 71.9 yrs; non-Indigenous males 80.6 yrs; First Nations females 75.6 yrs; non-Indigenous females 83.8 yrs. The male gap was 11.4 years in 2005–2007 and is 8.8 years now.

provenance.label: Source
provenance.value: ABS / Productivity Commission, Closing the Gap dashboard

slides.intro: Read the chart, then answer each task and reveal the model response.

tasks.question: What is the gap in life expectancy (in years) for males? For females?
tasks.model: Males: about 8.8 years (80.6 − 71.9). Females: about 8.2 years (83.8 − 75.6).

tasks.question: Describe the overall pattern the data shows.
tasks.model: First Nations people, both male and female, have a markedly lower life expectancy than non-Indigenous Australians, and in both groups females outlive males.

tasks.question: The male gap was 11.4 years in 2005–2007 and is 8.8 years now. Is the gap closing — and fast enough to reach equality by 2031?
tasks.model: The gap is narrowing (11.4 → 8.8 years), so there is progress. However, the rate is too slow: closing 2.6 years in roughly 15 years will not eliminate an 8.8-year gap by 2031, so the target is not on track.

slides.title: What drives the health gap?

source.label: Source B — Sources of the health gap (animated chart embeds here)
source.transcript: Estimated share of the health gap explained by social factors: Employment 14%; Household income 13%; Education 9%; Other factors (healthcare access, racism, environment, history) 64%.

provenance.label: Source
provenance.value: AIHW, Size and sources of the health gap

slides.intro: Use the chart to answer each task, then reveal the model response.

tasks.question: Which single social factor explains the largest share of the health gap?
Add up employment, income and education. What share of the gap do these 'social determinants' explain?
Why might improving jobs, income and education help close the health gap? Explain the link.
tasks.model: Secure jobs and higher income let people afford healthcare, healthy food and stable housing, while education improves health literacy and access to better-paid work. Because these social determinants shape health outcomes, improving them reduces the conditions that produce the gap.

slides.title: Why does the gap exist?
slides.hint: Hover a highlighted key term for its definition. Tap 'Reveal notes' for the lines to record.
body: [[The gap is rooted in colonisation: dispossession from Country, the forced removal of children known as the ==Stolen Generations==, and policies that damaged culture and community.]] These have ongoing effects today, called ==intergenerational trauma==.
[[Health is shaped by social determinants such as jobs, income, education, housing and access to services.]] Where these are unequal, health outcomes are unequal too.
[[Direct and systemic racism can reduce access to healthcare, housing, education and employment, which harms health and wellbeing.]]

[[Connection to family, community, Country and culture, together with ==self-determination==, all protect health and wellbeing.]] This is why community-controlled organisations and shared decision-making are central to closing the gap.

keyTerms.definition: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families under past government policies.
Harm passed down through generations when the effects of past events, like child removal, continue to affect families and communities today.
The right of peoples to make decisions about their own lives, communities and futures.

slides.title: Who should decide how to close the gap?
slides.question: Using the three-group role-play (government, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, other Australians), **evaluate** whether community-led solutions are the best way to close the gap, and whether the strategy is working.

stimulus.label: Activity
stimulus.text: The role-play has three groups: the government, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, and other Australians. Build your answer paragraph by paragraph.

slides.scaffoldLabel: Build your response paragraph by paragraph

paragraphs.label: Group concerns
paragraphs.guide: In your own words, what is each group's main concern?
paragraphs.model: Government has committed to equality and set targets, but plans have struggled with funding and follow-through. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities live with the gap and know what they need, and want a genuine say and resources. Other Australians mostly enjoy better outcomes. The key tension is who holds the power to decide.

paragraphs.label: Why community-led
paragraphs.guide: Why might community-led programs work better than programs designed only by government?
paragraphs.model: Communities understand their own needs, culture and context, so programs are more relevant and trusted. Self-determination is itself a protective factor for health. Top-down programs have often failed because they were not designed with the people they affect.

paragraphs.label: Evaluation
paragraphs.guide: Based on today's data, is the Closing the Gap strategy working? Give evidence for and against.
paragraphs.model: For: some targets are improving or on track (e.g. healthy birthweight reached 89.6%) and the life-expectancy gap is smaller than in 2005–2007. Against: the life-expectancy target is not on track for 2031, and some targets (out-of-home care, incarceration) are worsening. A strong answer weighs both sides before reaching a judgement.
